title: How many CPD credits do pharmacists need in Australia?
description: The Pharmacy Board of Australia CPD standard explained: 40 credits a year, Group 1 to 3 weighting, records, absences, and the 2026 proposal to move to hours.
shortAnswer: The Pharmacy Board of Australia requires every pharmacist with general registration to plan their continuing professional development and complete at least 40 CPD credits in each 12 month period ending 30 September. At least 20 credits must come from Group 2 or Group 3 activities, which earn two and three credits an hour. Pharmacists declare compliance at renewal, keep records for three full CPD periods, and may be audited by Ahpra.
keyTakeaways: The Registration standard: Continuing professional development has applied since December 1, 2015 and requires 40 CPD credits per CPD period, October 1 to September 30.

Credits are weighted: Group 1 (information without assessment) earns one credit an hour, Group 2 (with assessment) two, and Group 3 (practice improvement) three. No more than 20 credits may come from Group 1.
There is no pro rata reduction for part-time work or part-year practice, and excess credits cannot be rolled over.
In-house workplace education can count when it meets a need in the pharmacist's CPD plan, but supervising interns and students is practice, not CPD.

As at November 2026, Ahpra and 14 National Boards, including the Pharmacy Board, have consulted on a common standard of 20 hours a year that would replace the credit system if health ministers approve it.
regulator: Pharmacy Board of Australia, supported by the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (Ahpra)
appliesTo: Pharmacists with general registration, and applicants for general registration
Pharmacy interns with provisional registration, who meet the annual requirement during their internship
Community pharmacy owners, hospital pharmacy departments and other employers that provide or fund CPD for pharmacists

sections.heading: What does the Pharmacy Board's CPD standard require?

blocks.text: The standard requires two things: an annual CPD plan and at least 40 CPD credits in each CPD period. The Pharmacy Board of Australia's [Registration standard: Continuing professional development](https://www.pharmacyboard.gov.au/Registration-Standards.aspx), dated December 1, 2015 and approved by the Australian Health Workforce Ministerial Council on August 27, 2015, applies to applicants for general registration and all registered pharmacists, but not to pharmacists with non-practising registration or students.

To meet the standard a pharmacist must plan CPD each year by reflecting on their scope of practice against the National Competency Standards Framework for Pharmacists in Australia, identifying development needs and choosing activities to meet them. They must then "complete CPD activities that have an aggregate value of 40 or more CPD credits during each 12-month CPD period ending 30 September". Activities must be relevant to the pharmacist's scope of practice, of significant intellectual or practical content, delivered by qualified people or drawn from reputable sources, and must address development needs "upon reflection of how the activity has impacted your practice".

The duty rests on section 128 of the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law. The standard states that failing to undertake the required CPD "is not an offence but may be behaviour for which health, conduct or performance action may be taken", and that the Board can impose conditions or refuse registration or renewal (sections 82, 83 and 112). The cross-board picture is set out on the page about [Ahpra CPD registration standards](/regulations/ahpra-cpd-registration-standards).

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects the Pharmacy Board's standard, guidelines and consultation pages as at November 2026. The CPD guidelines were amended on April 10, 2026. A proposed replacement standard had been consulted on but not approved at that date.

sections.heading: How are CPD credits calculated for pharmacists?

blocks.text: Credits are calculated per hour and weighted by how much the activity tests or changes practice. The Board's [Guidelines on continuing professional development](https://www.pharmacyboard.gov.au/documents/default.aspx?record=WD15%2f18499&dbid=AP&chksum=H3lV5PqPKFCPuVIkiJyUkA%3d%3d) define three groups.

blocks.caption: Pharmacy Board of Australia CPD activity groups (source: Guidelines on continuing professional development)
head: Group
Board descriptor
Examples given by the Board
Credits per hour
rows: Attending CPD presentations, Grand Rounds or conferences without interaction; reading journals without a successful assessment; researching an issue for an individual patient
Knowledge or skills improved with assessment
Assessed online modules or journal reading with a defined pass mark; credentialing by examination; formal postgraduate courses; interactive workshops; case studies

Leading a workplace quality improvement activity such as a drug utilization review; implementing and evaluating a protocol identified through CPD; preparing a peer-reviewed article or conference paper

blocks.text: At least 20 of the 40 credits must come from Group 2 or Group 3, so a pharmacist cannot meet the standard on passive attendance alone. Twenty hours of Group 1 activity plus ten hours of assessed Group 2 activity reaches 40 credits; so does a single Group 3 project of just over 13 hours, although the Board "strongly suggests" not earning all credits from one event or source. The guidelines also remind pharmacists to maintain competence in the two universal domains of the competency framework: professional and ethical practice, and communication, collaboration and self-management.

Accreditation of activities is optional. The guidelines say the Board "has not set a mandatory requirement for a proportion of a pharmacist's CPD activities to be accredited CPD". For non-accredited activity, the pharmacist must judge quality and relevance, and the Board warns that activities "susceptible to commercial bias, such as sponsor-driven product detailing to pharmacists, are unlikely to be of sufficient quality". The April 10, 2026 amendment removed outdated content about the Australian Pharmacy Council authorizing organizations to accredit CPD activities.

sections.heading: When must pharmacists complete and declare CPD?

blocks.text: The CPD period runs from October 1 to September 30, and pharmacists declare whether they met the standard when they renew general registration. The Board's FAQ for pharmacists and interns states that renewal is due on November 30, two months after the CPD period closes.

items: **No pro rata.** The FAQ says the amount of CPD does not depend on hours worked, and there are no pro rata concessions for practicing only part of a registration period.
**No rollover.** Credits above 40 cannot be carried into the next period. Only activities completed between October 1 and September 30 count.

**No advance exemption.** A pharmacist who will fall short cannot seek an exemption before renewal. They must explain the shortfall in a letter with the renewal application, with a record of the CPD done. The Board may then renew without conditions, renew with conditions or refuse registration.

**Interns.** Pharmacy interns meet the annual requirement during their internship, which may not match the October to September period, and CPD done as an intern in the previous 12 months counts toward the first general registration renewal.

sections.heading: Does workplace training count toward pharmacist CPD?

blocks.text: Yes, when it addresses a learning need in the pharmacist's own CPD plan. The Board's FAQ answers "Can I include in-house CPD provided by my workplace?" with yes, and names hospital grand rounds, pharmacist continuing education meetings and workplace quality improvement activities as commonly counted.

The FAQ draws a firm line between learning and practice. Supervising interns and students "is part of day-to-day practice for supervising pharmacists, and is not CPD", although developing and delivering new teaching material can be. Delivering the same presentation again earns no further credits. Learning about therapeutic drug monitoring is CPD; checking a patient's phenytoin level and advising the prescriber is practice. A first aid refresher taken to keep a certificate valid can be claimed, which differs from the nursing rule that routine annual CPR training does not count.

For a pharmacy employer, this means workplace programs are worth designing so they can be claimed. A Group 3 project, such as a medication safety audit that the pharmacist plans, implements and evaluates, earns three credits an hour and also produces evidence for the service's own quality system, for example under the [NSQHS Standards](/regulations/nsqhs-standards-workforce-training) in a hospital.

sections.heading: What CPD records must a pharmacist keep?

blocks.text: Pharmacists should keep records for the previous three full CPD periods, and each record must contain specific fields. The standard says "You should maintain records of your CPD activity undertaken during the previous three full CPD periods", and the guidelines list the fields an audited pharmacist must provide.

items: Area identified as requiring development, with the relevant competencies from the competency standards framework
Start and finish date of the activity
Type of activity, such as journal article, seminar or workshop
How the activity has impacted practice
Pharmacy Board of Australia CPD credits claimed

blocks.text: Audited pharmacists may also need to produce their CPD plan and evidence of participation. The Board's [audit page](https://www.pharmacyboard.gov.au/Registration/Audit.aspx) says random samples are audited periodically through the year, and that an audit notice includes a checklist of the supporting documents required. The guide on [preparing training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) explains how an employer can structure attendance records so these fields are easy to complete.

sections.heading: What happens after a break from practice?

blocks.text: A pharmacist away from practice for one to three years must complete at least one year's quota of CPD relevant to their intended scope before recommencing, and must also meet the Board's recency of practice standard. The guidelines say an absence of more than three years "is not regarded by the Board as a temporary absence", so those pharmacists must meet the recency of practice standard and any supporting guidelines. During a break a pharmacist may choose not to do CPD, but the FAQ makes clear they must be up to date before returning.

sections.heading: Will pharmacists move from credits to hours?

blocks.text: Possibly. As at November 2026 the Pharmacy Board is one of 14 National Boards that consulted, with Ahpra, on a common CPD registration standard. The consultation opened on May 15, 2026 and closed on July 17, 2026, and the Board's [past consultations page](https://www.pharmacyboard.gov.au/News/Past-Consultations.aspx) lists the materials.

Ahpra's [consultation paper](https://www.ahpra.gov.au/documents/default.aspx?record=WD26%2f36029&dbid=AP&chksum=cSwA9u%2bcNJjI79QEoYPEog%3d%3d) notes that all boards set requirements in hours "except the Pharmacy Board which currently requires 40 CPD credits per year". The draft would require at least 20 hours each registration year, including 5 hours of interactive CPD with other practitioners, a CPD portfolio of goals, activities and reflections kept for five years, and an additional 10 hours for practitioners holding an endorsement for scheduled medicines. It would not set mandatory topics or minimum hours for activity types, which would end the Group 2 and Group 3 minimum.

The extra 10 hours matters because the Board separately consulted from April 20 to June 15, 2026 on a draft endorsement for scheduled medicines for pharmacists, and was reviewing submissions as at November 2026. If both proposals proceed, endorsed pharmacists would carry a larger CPD load than other pharmacists. Ahpra says practitioners would get substantial notice and transitional arrangements before any revised standard takes effect, so the 40 credit standard remains the rule until then.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: For pharmacy clients, Knowledge Foundry links each workplace learning activity to the competencies it addresses and the Board activity group its design supports, so the attendance record already carries the fields an audited pharmacist must report. If the credit system gives way to hours, the activity group attribute can be retired without rebuilding the underlying competency links.

faqs.q: Do part-time pharmacists need fewer CPD credits?
faqs.a: No. The Pharmacy Board's FAQ says the amount of CPD required does not depend on the hours a pharmacist works, and there is no pro rata concession for practicing only part of a registration period. A pharmacist who practises at any time in the period must meet the full 40 credit requirement.

faqs.q: Does CPD have to be accredited?
faqs.a: No. The guidelines say the Board has not set a mandatory proportion of accredited CPD, although it may do so after a future review. Accreditation tells the pharmacist an activity has been reviewed for quality and relevance; for non-accredited activities the pharmacist must make that judgment and record the accreditation status in their log.

faqs.q: Can a pharmacist count CPD done overseas?
faqs.a: In some cases. The FAQ says pharmacists who held limited registration before general registration, for example those who practised in the United Kingdom, Ireland, Canada or the United States, can count CPD undertaken overseas toward the annual requirement for general registration.

faqs.q: Does reading a journal count, and how many credits does it earn?
faqs.a: Reading a journal without a successful assessment is a Group 1 activity worth one credit per hour. Completing a structured assessment with a defined pass mark on that reading moves it to Group 2, worth two credits per hour. The FAQ advises that a given article should not appear more than once in an annual record.

Ahpra audits on behalf of the Pharmacy Board, using a nationally consistent approach across the National Boards. Randomly selected pharmacists receive an audit notice with a checklist and must provide their CPD plan and records supporting the declaration made at renewal. Compliance may also be checked when the Board receives a notification.
